title: Revised Julian Calendar
intro: A modern refinement of the Julian leap-year rule, proposed by Milutin Milanković in 1923, that stays very close to the Gregorian calendar for many centuries.
summary: Twelve familiar months. Century years are leap years only for two remainders in a repeating 900-year cycle.
origin: The Revised Julian calendar was devised in 1923 for Orthodox calendar reform. Different churches and communities have adopted different calendars for different purposes.
structure: Ordinary years follow the four-year leap rhythm, except that century years are leap only when their remainder upon division by 900 is 200 or 600.
pattern_note: Century years outside the two approved 900-year remainders are not leap years, even when divisible by four.
history: The Revised Julian system sought a very accurate solar calendar without retaining the original Julian calendar's accumulated seasonal drift. Its use in churches is not universal.
example: Year 2000 is leap in this rule, but year 2800 is not; Gregorian 2800 is a leap year. The systems thus eventually diverge.
limits: Dates before formal twentieth-century adoption are mathematical back-projections. Church observance and Paschal (Easter) calculations can involve separate rules.
